goldens.comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
goldens.reasoning: C1 flags the same side effects inside a predicate method.

goldens.comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.
goldens.reasoning: No candidate points out the regex domain-boundary bypass. C3 is about malformed emails, which is a different problem.

goldens.comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
goldens.reasoning: C2 flags the same case-sensitivity bypass.

candidates: should_block? is a predicate method but has write side effects (increments match_count, sets last_match_at, saves record), violating command-query separation; callers expect a ? method to be a pure read but every invocation silently mutates the database
Normalize the email before querying in BlockedEmail.should_block?; otherwise blocked addresses can be bypassed by changing case
EmailValidator no longer rejects malformed email addresses, so validates :email, email: true can now accept values like sam@sam or sam
